name: NDA (Non-Disclosure Agreement)
description: Comprehensive playbook for reviewing non-disclosure agreements, covering confidentiality obligations, permitted disclosures, and term provisions.
content:
# NDA Review Playbook

## Purpose
Review non-disclosure agreements to protect confidential information while ensuring business flexibility.

## Key Review Points

### 1. Parties and Definitions
- Verify correct legal names of all parties
- Review definition of "Confidential Information" for breadth
- Check for mutual vs. unilateral obligations
- Ensure clarity on what constitutes confidential vs. non-confidential information

### 2. Scope of Confidentiality
- Assess reasonableness of confidentiality obligations
- Review exceptions (public domain, independently developed, etc.)
- Check for residuals clause that may be too broad
- Verify permitted disclosures (legal requirements, advisors, etc.)

### 3. Term and Termination
- Review duration of confidentiality obligations (2-5 years typical)
- Check if term is reasonable for the business context
- Assess survival provisions post-termination
- Review return/destruction obligations

### 4. Use Restrictions
- Verify permitted uses align with business purpose
- Check for restrictions on reverse engineering
- Review employee/contractor disclosure limitations
- Assess non-solicitation or non-compete provisions (if any)

### 5. Remedies and Liability
- Review availability of injunctive relief
- Check for liquidated damages or limitation of liability
- Assess indemnification provisions
- Review dispute resolution mechanisms

### 6. General Provisions
- Verify governing law and jurisdiction
- Check for assignment restrictions
- Review amendment and waiver provisions
- Assess notice requirements

## Red Flags
- Indefinite confidentiality terms
- Overly broad definitions of confidential information
- Restrictions on hiring employees
- Unilateral modification rights
- Unreasonable geographic or time restrictions

## Negotiation Points
- Narrow definition of confidential information
- Reasonable term (3-5 years standard)
- Mutual obligations if appropriate
- Clear carve-outs for independent development
- Reasonable remedies without excessive penalties

name: SaaS Agreement
description: Expert playbook for reviewing Software-as-a-Service agreements, including licensing, data protection, SLAs, and termination provisions.
content:
# SaaS Agreement Review Playbook

## Purpose
Review SaaS agreements to ensure appropriate service levels, data protection, and business continuity.

## Key Review Points

### 1. Service Description and Scope
- Verify detailed description of services provided
- Review any service level commitments (SLAs)
- Check for limitations on users, data volume, or usage
- Assess availability guarantees and uptime commitments
- Review support and maintenance obligations

### 2. Fees and Payment Terms
- Review pricing structure (per user, tiered, usage-based)
- Check for price increase provisions and caps
- Assess payment terms and late payment penalties
- Review any setup or implementation fees
- Check for automatic renewal and price escalation

### 3. Data Rights and Privacy
- Verify data ownership provisions (customer owns data)
- Review data security and encryption requirements
- Check compliance with GDPR, CCPA, or other regulations
- Assess data portability and export rights
- Review data retention and deletion obligations
- Check for restrictions on data use by provider

### 4. Intellectual Property
- Verify customer retains ownership of customer data
- Review provider's IP ownership of platform
- Check for any IP assignment or licensing provisions
- Assess restrictions on reverse engineering
- Review feedback and improvement rights

### 5. Service Levels and Remedies
- Review uptime guarantees (99.9% typical)
- Check for service credits or refunds for downtime
- Assess exclusions from SLA calculations
- Review incident response and resolution times
- Check for performance monitoring and reporting

### 6. Term and Termination
- Review initial term and renewal provisions
- Check for termination rights (for cause and convenience)
- Assess notice periods for termination
- Review data retrieval rights upon termination
- Check for post-termination assistance obligations

### 7. Limitation of Liability
- Review liability caps (often 12 months fees)
- Check for carve-outs from limitations
- Assess consequential damages exclusions
- Review indemnification provisions
- Check for insurance requirements

### 8. Security and Compliance
- Review security certifications (SOC 2, ISO 27001)
- Check for security audit rights
- Assess incident notification requirements
- Review compliance with industry standards
- Check for vulnerability management obligations

## Red Flags
- No SLA or weak uptime guarantees
- Provider claims ownership of customer data
- No data export or portability rights
- Excessive liability limitations
- Automatic renewal without notice
- No termination for convenience
- Weak security commitments

## Negotiation Points
- Strong SLA with meaningful credits
- Clear data ownership and portability
- Reasonable liability caps with carve-outs
- Termination for convenience with reasonable notice
- Security audit rights
- Data processing agreement for GDPR compliance
- Price increase caps

name: Employment Agreement
description: Comprehensive playbook for reviewing employment agreements, covering compensation, duties, restrictive covenants, and termination provisions.
content:
# Employment Agreement Review Playbook

## Purpose
Review employment agreements to protect both employer and employee interests while ensuring legal compliance.

## Key Review Points

### 1. Position and Duties
- Verify job title and reporting structure
- Review description of duties and responsibilities
- Check for exclusivity requirements
- Assess location and remote work provisions
- Review any relocation requirements

### 2. Compensation and Benefits
- Review base salary and payment schedule
- Check for bonus or incentive compensation
- Assess equity grants (options, RSUs, etc.)
- Review benefits (health, retirement, vacation)
- Check for expense reimbursement policies
- Assess severance provisions

### 3. Term and Termination
- Review at-will vs. term employment
- Check termination provisions (cause, without cause)
- Assess notice requirements
- Review severance obligations and conditions
- Check for change of control provisions
- Assess resignation requirements

### 4. Restrictive Covenants
- Review non-compete provisions (scope, duration, geography)
- Check non-solicitation of customers/employees
- Assess non-disparagement provisions
- Review confidentiality obligations
- Check for garden leave provisions
- Assess enforceability under state law

### 5. Intellectual Property
- Review IP assignment provisions
- Check for work-made-for-hire clauses
- Assess carve-outs for prior inventions
- Review disclosure obligations for inventions
- Check for moral rights waivers

### 6. Confidentiality and Data Protection
- Review confidentiality obligations
- Check for trade secret protection
- Assess return of property obligations
- Review data privacy compliance
- Check for social media and communication policies

### 7. Dispute Resolution
- Review arbitration or litigation provisions
- Check for jury trial waivers
- Assess governing law and venue
- Review fee-shifting provisions
- Check for class action waivers

### 8. Other Provisions
- Review entire agreement clause
- Check for amendment procedures
- Assess assignment restrictions
- Review survival provisions
- Check for compliance with employment laws

## Red Flags
- Overly broad non-compete (time, geography, scope)
- Unreasonable IP assignment (covers personal projects)
- Weak severance provisions
- Unilateral modification rights
- Mandatory arbitration with employer-favorable terms
- No protection for whistleblowing
- Violations of state wage laws

## Negotiation Points
- Reasonable non-compete (6-12 months, limited geography)
- Carve-outs for personal projects in IP assignment
- Severance protection (especially for executives)
- Clear bonus/equity terms with acceleration
- Reasonable notice period for termination
- Mutual non-disparagement
- Choice of law favorable to employee

## State-Specific Considerations
- California: Non-competes generally unenforceable
- Massachusetts: Non-competes limited by statute
- Illinois: Income threshold for non-competes
- Colorado: Restrictions on non-competes
- Check local wage and hour laws
- Review state-specific confidentiality protections

name: M&A Asset Purchase Agreement
description: Expert playbook for reviewing asset purchase agreements in M&A transactions, covering purchase price, representations, and closing conditions.
content:
# M&A Asset Purchase Agreement Review Playbook

## Purpose
Review asset purchase agreements to ensure proper risk allocation, clear asset transfer, and protection of client interests.

## Key Review Points

### 1. Transaction Structure
- Verify assets being purchased (tangible and intangible)
- Review excluded assets
- Check for assumed liabilities vs. excluded liabilities
- Assess allocation of purchase price under IRC Section 1060
- Review any earnout or contingent consideration

### 2. Purchase Price and Payment
- Review total purchase price and components
- Check for working capital adjustments
- Assess earnout provisions and calculation methodology
- Review escrow or holdback amounts
- Check for purchase price allocation
- Assess payment terms and conditions

### 3. Representations and Warranties
- Review seller representations (organization, authority, etc.)
- Check financial statement representations
- Assess asset-specific representations (title, condition)
- Review intellectual property representations
- Check for material contract representations
- Assess employee and benefit representations
- Review litigation and compliance representations
- Check for bring-down requirements at closing

### 4. Covenants
- Review pre-closing covenants (conduct of business)
- Check for exclusivity or no-shop provisions
- Assess cooperation obligations (due diligence, approvals)
- Review post-closing covenants (non-compete, transition)
- Check for employee non-solicitation
- Assess confidentiality obligations

### 5. Conditions to Closing
- Review buyer conditions (due diligence, approvals)
- Check seller conditions
- Assess material adverse change (MAC) provisions
- Review regulatory approval requirements
- Check for third-party consent requirements
- Assess financing conditions (if applicable)

### 6. Indemnification
- Review scope of indemnification obligations
- Check for survival periods (18-24 months typical)
- Assess caps on indemnification (often purchase price)
- Review baskets and deductibles (tipping vs. dollar-one)
- Check for carve-outs from caps (fraud, taxes, etc.)
- Assess exclusive remedy provisions
- Review claims procedures and time limits

### 7. Closing and Post-Closing
- Review closing deliverables (bills of sale, assignments)
- Check for transition services agreement
- Assess employee offer letters and WARN Act compliance
- Review assumption agreements
- Check for estoppel certificates and consents
- Assess post-closing adjustment procedures

### 8. Termination
- Review termination rights (mutual, buyer, seller)
- Check for outside date
- Assess break-up fees or reverse break-up fees
- Review effect of termination on confidentiality

## Red Flags
- Vague asset descriptions
- Broad assumed liability provisions
- Weak or qualified representations
- Short survival periods for key representations
- Low indemnification caps
- Broad MAC definitions favoring seller
- Missing third-party consents
- Inadequate employee protections

## Negotiation Points
- Clear asset and liability schedules
- Strong representations with limited qualifiers
- Reasonable survival periods (18-24 months)
- Adequate indemnification caps (50-100% of purchase price)
- Reasonable baskets (0.5-1% of purchase price)
- Carve-outs from indemnification caps for fraud
- Specific performance rights for unique assets
- Transition services agreement for continuity

## Due Diligence Alignment
- Ensure representations cover key due diligence findings
- Address material issues discovered in diligence
- Verify disclosure schedules are complete
- Check for updates to representations at closing
- Ensure indemnification covers undisclosed liabilities

name: Commercial Lease Agreement
description: Comprehensive playbook for reviewing commercial real estate lease agreements, covering rent, maintenance, and tenant rights.
content:
# Commercial Lease Agreement Review Playbook

## Purpose
Review commercial lease agreements to ensure favorable terms for tenant operations and flexibility.

## Key Review Points

### 1. Premises and Use
- Verify exact description of leased premises
- Review permitted uses and restrictions
- Check for exclusive use provisions
- Assess common area definitions and access
- Review parking allocations
- Check for signage rights

### 2. Term and Renewal
- Review initial term and commencement date
- Check for renewal options and terms
- Assess notice requirements for renewal
- Review rent adjustments upon renewal
- Check for early termination rights
- Assess expansion or contraction options

### 3. Rent and Operating Expenses
- Review base rent and payment schedule
- Check for rent escalations (fixed, CPI, fair market)
- Assess operating expense pass-throughs (NNN, modified gross)
- Review CAM charges and reconciliation procedures
- Check for expense caps or stops
- Assess tax and insurance pass-throughs
- Review audit rights for operating expenses

### 4. Tenant Improvements and Alterations
- Review tenant improvement allowance
- Check for approval requirements for alterations
- Assess restoration obligations at lease end
- Review ownership of improvements
- Check for construction coordination requirements

### 5. Maintenance and Repairs
- Review allocation of maintenance responsibilities
- Check for structural vs. non-structural repairs
- Assess HVAC and system maintenance
- Review common area maintenance obligations
- Check for landlord repair obligations and timelines

### 6. Insurance and Indemnification
- Review required insurance types and limits
- Check for additional insured requirements
- Assess waiver of subrogation provisions
- Review indemnification obligations
- Check for limitation of landlord liability

### 7. Default and Remedies
- Review events of default
- Check for notice and cure periods
- Assess landlord remedies (termination, damages)
- Review tenant remedies for landlord default
- Check for self-help provisions
- Assess late payment penalties

### 8. Assignment and Subletting
- Review restrictions on assignment and subletting
- Check for landlord consent requirements (not unreasonably withheld)
- Assess recapture rights
- Review profit-sharing on sublets
- Check for affiliate assignment rights

### 9. Casualty and Condemnation
- Review casualty restoration obligations
- Check for termination rights after casualty
- Assess rent abatement during restoration
- Review condemnation provisions and awards
- Check for partial vs. total taking rights

## Red Flags
- Vague premises description
- Unreasonable use restrictions
- Uncapped operating expenses
- No audit rights for CAM charges
- Landlord can terminate without cause
- Absolute prohibition on assignment/subletting
- Weak casualty termination rights
- Personal guarantees required

## Negotiation Points
- Clear premises description with square footage
- Broad permitted use clause
- Operating expense caps or stops
- Audit rights with landlord payment if overcharge
- Reasonable renewal options at fair market rent
- Assignment/subletting consent not unreasonably withheld
- Tenant termination rights after casualty
- Rent abatement for landlord-caused interruptions
- Exclusive use provisions if in retail center

name: Intellectual Property License Agreement
description: Expert playbook for reviewing IP license agreements, covering scope, royalties, warranties, and termination provisions.
content:
# IP License Agreement Review Playbook

## Purpose
Review intellectual property license agreements to ensure appropriate rights, protections, and business flexibility.

## Key Review Points

### 1. Licensed IP and Scope
- Verify clear description of licensed IP (patents, trademarks, copyrights, trade secrets)
- Review field of use restrictions
- Check for territorial limitations
- Assess exclusive vs. non-exclusive license
- Review sublicensing rights
- Check for improvements and derivative works rights

### 2. Grant of Rights
- Review specific rights granted (make, use, sell, import, etc.)
- Check for reservation of rights by licensor
- Assess whether license is transferable
- Review rights to modifications and improvements
- Check for rights to future IP developments
- Assess cross-license provisions

### 3. Royalties and Payments
- Review royalty structure (running royalty, lump sum, milestone)
- Check for minimum royalties or guarantees
- Assess royalty base and calculation methodology
- Review payment terms and reporting requirements
- Check for audit rights
- Assess currency and withholding tax provisions

### 4. Term and Termination
- Review initial term and renewal provisions
- Check for termination rights (for cause, convenience)
- Assess notice requirements
- Review post-termination rights and obligations
- Check for sell-off periods
- Assess survival provisions

### 5. Warranties and Representations
- Review licensor warranties (ownership, authority, non-infringement)
- Check for performance warranties
- Assess disclaimer of other warranties
- Review "as-is" provisions
- Check for warranty limitations

### 6. Indemnification and Liability
- Review indemnification for IP infringement claims
- Check for defense and settlement obligations
- Assess indemnification procedures and cooperation
- Review limitation of liability provisions
- Check for consequential damages exclusions
- Assess liability caps

### 7. IP Protection and Enforcement
- Review obligations to maintain IP rights
- Check for enforcement rights and obligations
- Assess cost allocation for enforcement
- Review settlement approval requirements
- Check for cooperation obligations in litigation

### 8. Confidentiality
- Review confidentiality obligations for proprietary information
- Check for exceptions to confidentiality
- Assess term of confidentiality obligations
- Review return/destruction obligations

### 9. Quality Control and Compliance
- Review quality control requirements (especially for trademarks)
- Check for approval rights over licensed products
- Assess compliance with laws and regulations
- Review marking requirements (patent numbers, ®, ™)
- Check for most favored nations provisions

## Red Flags
- Vague description of licensed IP
- Overly broad field of use restrictions
- No sublicensing rights
- Unilateral modification of royalty rates
- Weak or no indemnification for infringement
- Licensor can terminate without cause
- No rights to improvements
- Excessive quality control requirements

## Negotiation Points
- Clear scope of licensed IP with schedules
- Broad field of use or minimal restrictions
- Sublicensing rights with reasonable approval
- Reasonable royalty rates with caps
- Strong indemnification for infringement claims
- Termination only for material breach with cure period
- Rights to improvements and derivative works
- Audit rights for royalty verification
- Exclusive license in key territories or fields
- Reduction in royalties for invalid or unenforceable IP

## Special Considerations by IP Type
- **Patents**: Review claim scope, prosecution history, validity
- **Trademarks**: Check for quality control, goodwill ownership
- **Copyrights**: Assess moral rights, derivative works
- **Trade Secrets**: Review confidentiality measures, disclosure limitations

name: Force Majeure - Neutral Position
description: Balanced force majeure clause protecting both parties equally
taskContext:
You will be provided with an agreement containing force majeure wording for review. Your task is to evaluate the clause and ensure it maintains balance between both parties.

Force majeure excuses a party when an extreme external event makes performance impossible or commercially impracticable. Typical triggers include natural disasters, epidemics, war, terrorism, and sweeping government actions. Courts read these clauses narrowly, so the wording must list key events and include a broad catchall for unforeseen catastrophes.

A balanced clause suspends obligations during the event, keeps pre-event payments due, and lets either side terminate if the disruption continues beyond a reasonable period.

guidelines.title: Clause Existence
guidelines.instruction: If the draft has no force-majeure clause, insert one that follows the example below
guidelines.rationale: Without a force majeure clause, parties have no clear mechanism to handle extraordinary events, leading to disputes and potential breach claims for circumstances beyond anyone's control.

guidelines.title: Event Coverage
guidelines.instruction: If the listed events omit flood, fire, earthquake, epidemic or pandemic, war, terrorism, or broad government action, add the missing items and a general catchall for events beyond reasonable control
guidelines.rationale: Comprehensive event coverage ensures the clause applies to genuinely unforeseeable circumstances while the catchall prevents gaps in protection.

guidelines.title: Market Changes Exclusion
guidelines.instruction: If the clause treats routine market or price changes as force majeure, move that language to a hardship section or delete it
guidelines.rationale: Market fluctuations are foreseeable business risks, not force majeure events. Including them undermines the clause's enforceability and commercial purpose.

guidelines.title: Notice Timing
guidelines.instruction: If notice of the event is required later than five business days after discovery, shorten the period to five business days and add a prompt-notice trigger
guidelines.rationale: Prompt notice allows the non-affected party to plan alternatives and mitigate losses. Five days balances urgency with practical constraints.

guidelines.title: Supporting Evidence
guidelines.instruction: If the clause requires supporting documents, allow up to thirty days after the initial notice for the affected party to supply evidence of the event
guidelines.rationale: Thirty days provides reasonable time to gather documentation while preventing indefinite delays in substantiating the claim.

guidelines.title: Mitigation Duty
guidelines.instruction: If the clause lacks a duty on the affected party to use reasonable efforts to mitigate and resume performance, add that duty
guidelines.rationale: Requiring mitigation prevents parties from using force majeure as an excuse to abandon obligations when workarounds exist.

guidelines.title: Termination Trigger
guidelines.instruction: Set the termination trigger [Y] as follows: thirty consecutive days for short-term deals or goods and services that can be replaced quickly; sixty consecutive days for typical supply, services, or technology agreements; ninety consecutive days for long-term infrastructure, construction, or energy projects
guidelines.rationale: Termination rights must align with the deal's nature and the parties' ability to find alternatives. Shorter deals need faster exits; complex projects need more time.

guidelines.title: Early Termination Prevention
guidelines.instruction: If the clause lets either party terminate before [Y] consecutive days of force majeure, change it so obligations are only suspended until [Y] has passed
guidelines.rationale: Premature termination undermines the clause's purpose of preserving the relationship during temporary disruptions.

guidelines.title: Bilateral Termination Right
guidelines.instruction: If the clause offers no termination right after [Y] consecutive days, add a bilateral right to terminate on written notice once [Y] has passed, with no liability beyond amounts already due
guidelines.rationale: Both parties need an exit if the disruption becomes permanent. Bilateral rights maintain fairness and prevent one party from holding the other hostage.

guidelines.title: Pre-Event Payment Obligations
guidelines.instruction: If the clause excuses payment obligations that accrued before the force-majeure event, delete that language so past-due amounts remain payable
guidelines.rationale: Force majeure should not excuse debts already incurred. This protects the performing party's right to payment for work completed before the event.

exampleClause: Neither party is liable for any failure or delay in performing an obligation under this Agreement to the extent the failure or delay is caused by a Force Majeure Event beyond its reasonable control, provided that the affected party gives the other party prompt written notice, and in any event within five business days after becoming aware of the event. A Force Majeure Event includes flood, fire, earthquake, epidemic or pandemic, war, terrorism, governmental action, and any similar event beyond the affected party's reasonable control that makes performance impossible or impracticable. The affected party will use all reasonable efforts to mitigate the effects of the Force Majeure Event and to resume full performance. Obligations are suspended during the Force Majeure Event, but amounts due before the event remain payable. If the Force Majeure Event continues for more than [Y] consecutive days, either party may terminate this Agreement by written notice without further liability other than payment for obligations that accrued before the effective date of termination.

name: Force Majeure - Non-Affected Party Position
description: Force majeure clause protecting the party entitled to receive performance
taskContext:
You have been asked to review the force‑majeure wording in a bilateral commercial agreement. Our goal is to ensure the clause protects the party that is entitled to receive performance when the counterparty is disrupted (the Non‑Affected Party). The guidelines below make sure that (i) only genuine, narrowly defined events excuse performance, (ii) the affected party must act quickly, transparently and at its own cost to resume work, and (iii) the Non‑Affected Party can terminate or seek alternatives before the stand‑still causes material loss.

Force majeure excuses a party only when an extreme external event renders performance impossible despite diligent mitigation. Typical triggers include major natural disasters, declared epidemics, war, terrorism and binding government orders. Courts read these clauses narrowly, so the wording must list key events and exclude economic or supply‑chain excuses. A Non‑Affected‑Party clause requires prompt notice and proof, keeps payment obligations current, allows substitution or price adjustment and lets the Non‑Affected Party terminate early if service is unreliable.
guidelines: If the draft has no force‑majeure clause, insert one that follows the example below.

If the listed events include routine market changes, cost increases, cyber‑attack without system outage or supplier failures, delete those items. Keep the list to flood, fire, earthquake, government order expressly preventing performance, declared epidemic or pandemic, war or terrorism and a tightly worded catchall for events that make performance impossible despite reasonable mitigation.
Require the affected party to prove that the event directly caused the failure and could not have been avoided by reasonable back‑up plans or alternative sourcing.

Set notice at three business days from discovery. The notice must be in writing and include reasonable details of the event, its expected impact and the steps being taken to mitigate. Late or inadequate notice voids relief until corrected.
Require supporting evidence within fifteen days, such as government proclamations, third‑party certificates or insurance loss reports. If evidence is not supplied, force‑majeure relief lapses.

Impose a duty to use all reasonable efforts to overcome the effects, including sourcing from alternate facilities, expediting shipments or subcontracting, even at extra cost unless commercially unreasonable.
Keep payment obligations that fall due during the period on schedule. If performance is partially possible, require prorated price reduction or service‑credit scheme.
State that liquidated damages or service credits continue to accrue unless the affected party shows that mitigation was impossible.

Set the termination trigger [Y] as follows: thirty consecutive days for short‑term or easily substitutable goods and services; sixty consecutive days for typical supply, services or technology agreements; ninety consecutive days for long‑term infrastructure, construction or energy projects.
Allow the Non‑Affected Party to terminate immediately if the event appears permanent or if the affected party cannot provide satisfactory mitigation within ten business days of notice.
Permit the Non‑Affected Party to procure substitute goods or services during the suspension and offset reasonable extra costs against amounts otherwise payable to the affected party.
exampleClause:
"Neither party is liable for any failure or delay in performing an obligation under this Agreement to the extent the failure or delay is caused by a Force Majeure Event beyond its reasonable control and despite the exercise of all reasonable mitigation efforts, provided that the party claiming relief (the affected party) gives the other party written notice within three business days after becoming aware of the event. The notice must describe the event, its anticipated impact and mitigation steps. A Force Majeure Event is limited to flood, fire, earthquake, officially declared epidemic or pandemic, war, terrorism or a binding government order that expressly prevents performance, together with any similar event that renders performance objectively impossible even with reasonable back‑up measures. Within fifteen days after notice, the affected party will supply documentary evidence substantiating the claim. Failure to provide timely notice or evidence suspends relief until corrected.

The affected party will use all reasonable efforts, including alternative sourcing, expedited transport or subcontracting, to resume full performance as soon as practicable, regardless of additional cost unless commercially unreasonable. Payment obligations that fall due remain payable on schedule; if performance is partially hindered, the price will be reduced pro rata and service‑level credits will continue to apply. Liquidated damages and other remedies remain in effect unless the affected party demonstrates that timely mitigation was objectively impossible.

If the Force Majeure Event continues for more than [Y] consecutive days, or if the event appears permanent, the Non‑Affected Party may terminate this Agreement immediately on written notice without liability. During any suspension, the Non‑Affected Party may procure substitute goods or services, and any reasonable incremental cost will be recoverable from or offset against amounts payable to the affected party."

Payment obligations that fall due remain payable on schedule; if performance is partially hindered, the price will be reduced pro rata and service‑level credits will continue to apply. Liquidated damages and other remedies remain in effect unless the affected party demonstrates that timely mitigation was objectively impossible.

If the Force Majeure Event continues for more than [Y] consecutive days, or if the event appears permanent, the Non‑Affected Party may terminate this Agreement immediately on written notice without liability. During any suspension, the Non‑Affected Party may procure substitute goods or services, and any reasonable incremental cost will be recoverable from or offset against amounts payable to the affected party."

name: Force Majeure - Protected Party Position
description: Force majeure clause protecting the party whose performance is disrupted
taskContext:
You have been asked to review the force majeure wording in a bilateral commercial agreement. Our goal is to ensure the clause protects the party whose performance is disrupted by events outside its control while still letting either side exit cleanly if the stand‑still lasts too long. The guidelines below make sure that (i) a wide range of uncontrollable events excuse performance, (ii) the protected party faces minimal procedural burdens, and (iii) financial exposure is paused during the disruption.

Force majeure excuses a party when an extreme external event prevents or materially impedes performance. Typical triggers include natural disasters, epidemics, cyber‑attacks, war, terrorism, government embargoes, utility failures, and major supply shortages. Courts read these clauses narrowly, so the wording must name key events and include a broad catchall. A protected‑party clause suspends obligations during the event, defers payments that fall due, shields the party from damages, and lets either side terminate if the disruption persists.
guidelines: Include an anti red tape safeguard. Notice may be sent by email or other electronic means and no specific form or courier delivery is required. Only information reasonably available at the time must be provided.
If the draft has no force‑majeure clause, insert one that follows the example below.

If the listed events omit flood, fire, earthquake, epidemic or pandemic, cyber‑attack, labour or material shortage, war, terrorism, broad government action or utility failure, add the missing items and a broad catchall for events beyond reasonable control.
If the clause limits relief to events that make performance impossible, broaden it so that events preventing or materially impeding performance also qualify.
If notice of the event is required sooner than ten business days, extend the period to ten business days and add a saver that late notice caused by the event does not forfeit relief.
If the clause requires supporting documents, allow up to ninety days after the initial notice for the protected party to supply evidence of the event.

If the clause imposes a duty on the protected party to use all reasonable efforts, soften it to commercially reasonable efforts with no obligation to incur material extra cost or accept adverse terms.

Defer any payments that become due during the force‑majeure period until ten business days after performance resumes, and state that no penalties, liquidated damages or service credits accrue during suspension.

Set the termination trigger [Y] as follows: sixty consecutive days for short‑term deals or goods and services that can be replaced quickly; ninety consecutive days for typical supply, services or technology agreements; one hundred twenty consecutive days for long‑term infrastructure, construction or energy projects.
If the clause lets either party terminate before [Y] consecutive days of force majeure, change it so obligations are only suspended until [Y] has passed.

If the clause offers no termination right after [Y] consecutive days, add a bilateral right to terminate on written notice once [Y] has passed, with no liability beyond amounts already due before the force‑majeure event.
If the clause keeps payment obligations that accrue during the event payable on schedule, amend it to defer those payments.
exampleClause: "Neither party is liable for any failure or delay in performing an obligation under this Agreement to the extent the failure or delay is caused by a Force Majeure Event beyond its reasonable control, provided that the protected party gives the other party notice within ten business days after becoming aware of the event. Notice may be sent by email or any other electronic means and no particular form is required. The initial notice must contain only the information then reasonably available; supporting details will be supplied when practicable and in any event within ninety days. Delay in giving notice that is attributable to the event does not affect this relief. No additional steps or protocols are required to claim Force Majeure. A Force Majeure Event includes flood, fire, earthquake, epidemic or pandemic, cyber‑attack, shortage of labour, materials, power, or transport, war, terrorism, governmental action, utility failure, and any similar event beyond the protected party's reasonable control that prevents or materially impedes performance. The protected party will use commercially reasonable efforts to mitigate the effects of the Force Majeure Event and to resume full performance, but is not required to incur material extra cost or accept commercially unreasonable terms. Obligations, including payment obligations that would otherwise fall due during the Force Majeure Event, are suspended and deferred until ten business days after the event ends, and no damages, penalties, or service credits accrue while it lasts. If the Force Majeure Event continues for more than [Y] consecutive days, either party may terminate this Agreement on ten days written notice without further liability other than payment for obligations that accrued before the Force Majeure Event began."
